Files, directories and the directory tree
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
Before you learn commands for files, you need a picture of what a file is and how Linux organizes many files.
The working directory and paths
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
There is no mouse in the terminal to point at a file. You name a file by writing down its route through the tree.
Showing the contents of a directory
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
ls is the command people type most often at the command line: it shows what is in a directory.
Viewing files
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
Many files of a Linux system are text that you can read directly: configuration files, logs, instructions.
Creating files and directories
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
So far, you have only looked. From here on, you change the tree: you create directories, make files, write text into them and view the result as a tree.
Copying, moving, deleting
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
You do not only work with files; you also rearrange them: making a backup copy, changing a name, throwing away what is old.
The directory structure of Linux
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
In /, there are a good twenty directories with short, puzzling names. They follow a plan that is the same on almost all Linux systems.
Inodes and links
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
So far, a file name was simply the name of a file. This section looks underneath: the name and the file are two different things, connected only by an entry in the directory.
Storage devices and mounting
Linux and the Command Line · Chapter 3: Files, Directories and Paths
